div.head: THE Surest and Safest WAY OF THRIVING.

q.p: He that receiveth a Prophetprophet in the name of a Prophetprophet, shall receive a Prophetsprophets reward: and he that receiveth a righteous man in the name of a righteous man, shall receive a righteous mans reward.
And whosoever shall give unto one of these little ones, a cup of cold water onelyonly, in the name of a Discipledisciple, verily I say unto you, he shall in no wise lose his reward.

div.p:
THE troubles whereunto God bringeth his Ministersministers and Peoplepeople, though they be many and Greatgreat, yet are they not more, and greater, then the comforts which Hehe affordeth unto them, to support and encourage them in their troubles. Instance this Chapterchapter, and the Sermonsermon of Christ therein recorded, concerning those sore Trialstrials whereunto his Churchchurch and Childrenchildren should be brought. As any kind of affliction is foretold, a proper and peculiar consolation is usually annexed. Therefore to establish the hearts of his suffering Servantsservants, and to encourage their Succourers,
Hehe closes up Hishis Sermonsermon with the words of the text, wherein Hehe declareth not only that high account which he had of Hishis Ministersministers, and Peoplepeople themselves, but also of them who should yield any relief, of upon Hishis account shewshow kindness to them, assuring them; Thatthat he who receiveth a Prophetprophet in the name of a Prophetprophet, should receive a Prophetsprophets reward. Andand he that receiveth a righteous man in the name of a righteous man, should receive a righteous mans reward.

The words in brief contain, A Declaration of that great benefit, which they bring to themselves, who afford any relief, and succour to Ministersministers, or other Saintssaints; teaching, Thatthat there is no such way to fill our Treasurestreasures, as by emptying them for God.

For, the clearing of the words, I shall breifly shewshow you,
1. Who is here meant by a Prophetprophet. Andand who by a Righteousrighteous man.
2. What is meant by receiving them.
3. What is the Rewardreward which followeth thereupon.
I. For the first, who is here meant by a Prophetprophet; and who by a Righteousrighteous man.

By a Prophetprophet our Saviour here meaneth not onelyonly extraordinary Ministersministers, such as were immediatlyimmediately and extraordinarily inspired by the Holy Ghost; or who had extraordinary revelations to foretell things to come: but also ordinary Ministersministers of the word, and interpreters of the Scriptures, as IohJoh. 4. 44. Rev. 11. 18.

By Righteousrighteous men he meaneth his Saintssaints, or such as testifietestify their justification thorow faith in Christ, by their sanctification, and fruits of a good conscience, whom commonly the Scripture stilethstyleth Saintssaints.
II. For the Secondsecond, what is meant by receiving these?
For Answeranswer thereunto, you must know, Therethere are two things whereunto this receiving may have a respect.
1. To the word and message of a Ministerminister, and so it signifies, the hearkning to, and embracing their holy Counselcounsel and Doctrinedoctrine.

2. To the Person of a Ministerminister, and so it signifies the harbouring, or shewingshowing kindness to Himhim, as is evident from the instance of cold water, given unto a Prophetprophet, or Righteousrighteous man, expressed in the following verse. Both these are implyed under this phrase of receiving a Prophetprophet, viz. His Doctrinedoctrine, by embracing, and submitting to it: and his Person, by harbouring, succouring, and relieving him according to his need.

Byby the receiving a Prophetprophet, in the name of a Prophetprophet, is meant a a succouring and relieving him for his particular calling sake, eo nomine, because he is a Prophetprophet. So by receiving a righteous man, in the name of a righteous man, intendeth the same thing; namely, the relieving him, for his Generalgeneral callings sake, because he is a Christian a child of God, and a member of Christ.

III. For the third particular, what is here meant by the reward of a Prophetprophet, and of a righteous man? I Answeranswer, Thesethese phrases of receiving a Prophetsprophets, and of a Righteousrighteous mans reward, may be taken Actively, or Passively. Actively, for that reward which a Prophetprophet or a righteous man giveth. Passively, for that which is by God given to the one, and to the other. Thethe reward which a Prophetprophet giveth, is ministerially to preach the word of Reconciliationreconciliation to such as receive them, as Peter did to Cornelius, Actact. 10. 34. &etcc. To pray for them, as Abraham for Abimeleck, Gen. 20. 7, 17, Andand to bless them, as Melchisedec blessed Abraham, Gen. 17. 19.
The reward which a righteous man giveth is privately to instruct, and edifieedify, to pray for, and to be a good pattern, and example of righteousness, to such as entertain or otherwise relieve him.

Thethe reward which is given by God, to either of these, for that kindness which any shewshow unto them, is such a surpassing, and excellent weight of glory, as cannot be expressed by the tongue of men, or Angelsangels, yet different in degrees, as is evident, Dan. 12. 3.
Some take these phrases, Ofof receiving a Prophetprophet, and a righteous mans reward, in the former sense, Actively; and others, Passively. I conceive it may be taken in both.
The words thus explained do afford unto us several points of Doctrinedoctrine.
From the duty here expressed of receiving, and relieving Prophetsprophets, and righteous men, with the manner of setting it down, we may observe.
1. Doct. Thatthat all needful succour, and good entertainment is to be afforded to Ministersministers of the Gospel. Thisthis is the main and principal point intended.

2. Doct. Christian kindness is to be shewedshowed not only to Ministersministers, but also to all the members of Christ. Forfor our blessed Saviour contents not himself to have mentioned a Prophetprophet, but also addeth a righteous man.
These two sorts make up Thethe household of Faithfaith; to whom the Apostle exhorteth Christians especially to doedo good, Gal. 6. 10.
Q. Is our Charitycharity to extend no farther?

A. Yesyes, even to all that are in want, but especially to such as have a particular relation to Christ, as being his members, or Ministersministers; because Christ in them is after an especial manner succoured, and relieved. It will be therefore our wisdom to take notice of the extent of this duty, and in all we doedo, either for Christians or others, to see to it, that what we doedo, is done for the Lords, and for conscience-sake, to the one in compassion to his members, to the other in obedience to his will.

4. Doct. According to the kindness which we shewshow, shall our reward be. Hehe that receiveth, and relieveth a Prophetprophet, shall receive a Prophetsprophets reward. Andand he that receiveth and relieveth a righteous man, shall receive the reward of a righteous man.

q.p: And whosoever shall give to drink unto one of these little ones, a cup of cold water onelyonly in the name of a Discipledisciple, he shall in no wise lose his reward.

div.p: These words are added by our Saviour to the former to anticipate some Objectionsobjections, which might be made thereupon, as also more fully to explain the forementioned points.

1. ObjObi. Maymay be thus made, Thesethese Preacherspreachers and Professorsprofessors of the Gospel are but mean persons, and little in esteem, what great reward can be expected for entertaining them?

A. Asas little as they be, be they as inconsiderable and contemptible as the proud world make them, yet are they not so little in the eyes of Lord, but that he will reward all such as are friendly to them.
2. ObjObi. I my self am but poor, and can doedo but little for them.

A. Thoughthough thy kindness be never so small, as small as a cup of water, and that cold, taken out of the Riverriver, without any pains or cost to heat it, yea but ONE cup full thereof, and no more, (supposing that to be the most thou canst doedo for them) yet it shall be rewarded by him, who more respecteth the willingness of the Givergiver, then the greatness of the Giftgift.
The greatest difficulty in the words is who are here meant by little ones, for whose sake the reward is promised.
By little ones, our Saviour meaneth no other than such in the foregoing verse, he had stiledstyled Prophetsprophets and righteous ones.
They are called Little ones in two respects.

list.item: 1. In regard of the worlds esteem of them.
2. In regard of their own account of themselves.

div.p: First, Theythey are little in the worlds eye. Thethe world which judgeth not according to inward worth, have them in low esteem. It fares with the servants, as it fared with their Mastermaster, they are despised, and rejected, and troden under foot of men. Of old they were accounted Desolate, and forsaken, Isa. 62. 4. In the Apostles time, the filth of the world, the of scouring of all things, 1 Cor. 4. 13. Experience of all ages verifieth as much. And among other ages ours giveth not the least evidence.

That comfort and contentment which God's people find in the Lord, and the light of his countenance, yea that hope they have of finding grace in his eyes, make them the less to mind, and seek after the honour, wealth, and promotions of the world, and commonly they have but little of it. Now the world judgeth according to outward, earthly, worldly glory, it discerneth not the spiritual glory of the Saintssaints, 1 IohJoh. 3. 1.

Judg not of men according to the worlds judgment: think not ever the more meanly of Saintssaints, because the world thinks so of them. They are highly favoured of the most Highhigh: they are such of whom the world is not worthy, they are the excellent ones, Psal. 16. 3: but what ever they be in deed, in the eye of the world they are but little ones.

Secondly, Theythey are little in their owneown eyes, Gen. 18. 27. weWe read how Abraham in speaking to God, stiles himself no better than Dust and ashes. Andand Gen. 32. 10. IacobJacob acknowledgeth himself unworthy, or, less than the least of Gods Merciesmercies.

The ground thereof may be because the Saintssaints best know themselves, since they more thorowlythoroughly, than other men, Searchsearch their hearts, and observe their ways, and compare themselves with the pure and perfect law of God, and take notice of their inward, Secretsecret corruptions, as well as of their outward and visible transgressions:
and thus come they to know more of themselves, then any other can, or may suspect of them. And this clearer sight of themselves brings them down, and lays them low. This made Saintsaint Paul to cry out, Rom. 7. 24. O wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death? Thisthis is a note of true grace, and of a sanctified heart. They are the poor in spirit, not the proud in Spirit, that are Christs blessed ones, Math. 5. 3. The false disciple thinketh highly of himself, and would be accounted not 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 a little one, like a true disciple of Christ; but 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉
Somesome great one, like to Simon Magus, Actact 8. 8, 9. This Spirit is a Satanicalsatanical Spirit. Try thy Spirit by this note, whether it be of God, or no.

But though all the Servantsservants of God are on the the forementioned account little ones, yet there are some among them less than others, as in regard of their offices, and stations in the Churchchurch, some are in higher, others in lower Officesoffices, some are in office, others not; Soso also in regard of their parts and gifts, and graces, some are strong, and others are weak; some the chief, others the least of Saintssaints: some as the head, and others but as the finger, or the foot: and 'tis probable the text hath the most special respect (and the Emphasisemphasis of it is the greater) to the least of all these little ones, and so the expression is Math. 25. 40. In as much as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren ye have done it unto me.

This I the rather take notice of it to give an hint to Christians in their Charitablecharitable distributions to have an eye to such Ministersministers or Christians as are more obscure, and less considerable in the Worldworld. Possibly when those of greater worth and remark may tast deeply of their bounty, every one almost hath a kindness for them: in the mean time there may be some poor hidden ones, whose worth is less, but their wants are greater, who being low in those gifs or graces which would commend them to the more publick notice, are almost buried in forgetfulness. Its true that by how much the more eminent the person is that is relieved (caeteris paribus) by so much the more excellent the work: yet special care should be taken that the more obscure and least deserving among all that belong to God be not forgotten.
The words thus explained, afford unto us two special poins of Doctrinedoctrine.
1. Doct. God taketh notice of every of his Saintssaints, even of the least of them, and of kindness shewedshowed to them.

Though IosephJoseph was but a lad, and sold as a slave, yet being one of the Churchchurch, one of the little ones, yea minimorum minimus; yet in AEgyptAegypt God takes notice of him, and of that kindness which was shewedshowed to him, Gen. 32. 5. Many other like examples are noted in the Scripture; but none more fit for our purpose, than the example of Lazarus, Luk. 16. 20. thoughThough he were a very poor beggar, and full of sores, and despised of Dives, and all his househol • d, yet God took such notice of him, as he made his Angelsangels attend him. Yea God took notice of the kindness which the Dogsdogs shewedshowed him, for their licking of his sores is recorded to all ages. Note those expressions of the Psalmistpsalmist, Psal. 40. 12. But I am poor and needy, yet the Lord thinketh upon me. Andand again Psal. 34. 6. This poor man cryed, and the Lord heard him, and saved him out of all his troubles.
Qu. If you ask, why the Lord taketh notice of every of his Saintssaints.

Ans. 1. Theythey are all his Childrenchildren, and of his household; therefore as a tender, and carefullcareful father, and Mastermaster, he careth for every one. Yea they are all members of the body of Christ. Now the head taketh care of every member, even the least, and taketh notice of every kindness done to any of them.

2. Theythey are all by reason of grace in them, as Iewelsjewels and precious stones; therefore as a provident IewellerJeweller he will look to every one of them. Yea that which often appeareth least may be of greater worth; as a little Diamond is of more Valuevalue than a far greater pebble.

This affordeth a singular ground of comfort to such as in this world are desolate, and forsaken: though they be left alone (as Elijah was 1 King 19. 10.) Andand as a Pelicanpelican in the wilderness: Oror an Owlowl of the Desertdesert, Oror as a sparrow alone upon the house top, as the Psalmistpsalmist expresseh, Psal. 102. 6, 7. yetYet is the Lord with them, and takes care of them. Now if the Lord be with us, and taketh care of us, Whatwhat need me fear?] Howhow should this encourage us to extend our charity to any one of the Saintssaints, and members of Christ, though mean and little in the world, and not able to recompencerecompense us: and though none take notice thereof, to consider that the Lord taketh notice, and will abundantly recompencerecompense every good work, yea the least kindness we do unto them. Heb. 6. 10. God is not unrighteous
to forget your work, and labour of love, which ye have shewedshowed towards his name, in that ye have ministredministered to the Saintssaints, and do minister, Wherewhere, Gods not forgetting their labour of love in ministringministering to the Saintssaints, doth imply, that as God taketh notice of their beneficence, Soso he is, and will be ever mindfullmindful of such and such persons to support and succour, and every way do them good.

And if God will thus remember those that remember the least of his, how will he take it that they are neglected? Beloved, how is it with Gods little ones at this day? Is it not very low with many, of them? God takes notice how very low it is; and whether you will or no, God will not forsake them; but (that I may use the words of Mordecai to EsterEsther, with some variation, EsterEsther. 4. 14.) Ifif you altogether hold your hand at this time, relief shall arise to them some other way, but you and your house (take heed that word be not verified upon you) shall be destroyed. But who knows whether you are come to your estates for such a time as this!

And thus I come to the Secondsecond and main point of Doctrinedoctrine, which riseth from the reward promised to such as shewshow the least kindness to a minister, or righteous man, though it be but a cup of cold water they shall in no wise lose their reward. Whencewhence we may observe.
2. Doct. Thatthat the least work of charity shewedshowed to a Ministerminister or righteous man, shall be abundantly recompensed, and that not only hereafter, but likewise here on earth.

Though our beneficence ought to extend unto all who are in want and come within the verge of our knowledge, and power, as Gal. 6. 10. According as we have opportunity, let us do good unto ALLall men; yet I confine my discourse here to Ministersministers, and righteous ones, because they only are implyed under those little ones mentioned in my text.

That mercifullmerciful men shall be abundantly recompencedrecompensed hereafter in heaven for their works of charity, there is no doubt, being so clearly expressed in the word of God, Luk. 16. 9. Makemake your selves friends of the Mammonmammon of unrighteousness, that when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting habitations Andand 1 Tim. 6. 17. Charge them that are rich in this world, that they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate, laying up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come, that they may lay hold of eternal life.

But the great question is concerning temporal reward, Whetherwhether Christian charity, rightly performed, shall be recompencedrecompensed here in this life with temporal blessings: Soso that what men give in a way of charity, there is ground to expect, it shall be here returned into their bosomesbosoms again with increase.

I deny not but a charitable man may become poor, and be reduced into some straights, through Suretiship, negligence in his Callingcalling, or in respect of some secret sin, wherein he liveth, which may justly bring a temporal curse upon him: Soso that his liberality in such cases may not be a sufficient fence against want and penury. But this I say, Thatthat as penuriousness towards the poor is the readiest way to poverty: Soso Christian charity, rightly performed, is the surest way to plenty and abundance, it being usually rewarded with temporal blessings here, as well as with eternal hereafter. Where is the man to be found, that is the poorer by what he hath given to the poor? How many are the instances of such which have met with some signal blessings from God in this life, as the reward of their liberality?

This may seem a paradox to many uncharitable men, that Givinggiving should be the surest way of getting, and that the more liberal any man is, the more likely he is to thrive and prosper in the world. Yetyet nothing more clearly laid down in the Scripture, and found to be true by the experience of multitudes of Gods people in all ages. Andand I am verily perswadedpersuaded, that there is seldomeseldom any man, that maketh conscience of this duty, who giveth out to the poor proportionably to what God hath bestowed on him, and with an honest, upright heart, but if he do observe the passages of Gods providence towards him, he shall find the same doubled, and redoubled upon him in temporal blessings, I dare challenge all the world to give one instance, or at least any considerable number of instances of any truly mercifullmerciful men, whose charity hath undone them. But as living wells the more they are drawn, the more freely they spring, and flow; Soso the substance of charitable men doth oftentimes, if not ordinarily, multiply in the very distribution; Eveneven as the five loaves, and few fishes did multiply in their breaking, and distributing. And the widdows Oyl increased by the pouring it out.
But these bare assertions being no full convictions: Forfor the better clearing the truth of this doctrine, I shall prove it by Scriptures, Examplesexamples, and Reasonsreasons.

1. For Scripture proofesproofs, there are very many both in the old, and Newnew-Testament. What the Apostle saith of Godlinessgodliness, 1 Tim. 4. 8. Itit is profitable unto all things, having the promise of this life, and of that which is to come. Thethe like I may say of Charitycharity, Itit is profitable unto all things, having promises of temporal blessings, as well as of Spiritualspiritual, and eternal.

Deut. 15. 10. Thouthou shalt surely give unto thy brother, and thy heart shall not be grieved when thou givest unto him; because that for this the Lord thy God shall bless thee in all thy workesworks, and in all that thou puttest thine hand unto. Itit is not thine own labour, or care, but the divine blessing that maketh rich, and of that blessing behold here's a Scripture-entail upon the liberal. And the like we have Pro. 3. • . 9, 10. Honour the Lord with thy substance, by giving out a portion thereof for the relief of the poor, Soso shall thy barns be filled with plenty, and as thy Barnes, so thy Shop, thy Cellers, warehouses, where thou bestowest thy goods, shall be filled with abundance: and thy presses shall burst out with new wine, this seemeth to be an hyperbolical expression, yet it signifieth no less then this, that Gods usuallusual way is to make good returns of all we lay out upon him and his; and that our wisest way both for ensuring, and improving what we have is to make our selves Creditorscreditors to his wanting Saintssaints.

A compassionate heart, and an helping hand will gather by expending; such giving is getting, such bounty is the most compendious way to plenty. Whereupon the wiseman addeth, Pro. 11. 24. Therethere is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; there is that withholdeth more then is meet, but it tendeth to poverty. Whowho is he, here, that scattereth? notNot he that wastes his estate upon his throat, his back and his belly, or with the Prodigal upon Harlots; but he that casteth his bread upon the waters, as the expression is Eccl. 11. 1. Hehe that disperseth and giveth to the poor, as Psal. 112. 9. thisThis is the scatterer in that text. And what of him? isIs he wasted? isIs he impoverished? Behold the quite contrary: the man is grown rich, he is encreasedincreased by scattering. Letlet him look to it, that withholdeth more than is meet: this is the more likely man of the two to be found shortly on the dunghil. If thou wilt secure thy self from beggery, keep not Gods beggers from thy door, nor send them away empty whose needs, though not their tongues, cry in thine ears, Givegive for the Lords sake. Fearfear not to loose by laying out. Thy laying up what thou shouldst
lay out hath the most danger in it. The divine curse may wither that in thine hand which thou holdest fast against the divine command.

In the following verse we read further, Thethe liberal soul shall be made fat. Thethe Soulsoul is often in Scripture taken to signifiesignify the Manman, and so it is here, and is the same, as the liberal man. To be made fat, signifies to prosper, to be full, and abound, or to grow rich in this worlds goods; and thus it shall be, if this Scripture may be credited.

The liberal Soulsoul] Itit is in the Hebrew, as you may find it noted in the Marginmargin, the Soulsoul of blessing, the merciful man is a blessing, and hath a blessing for such as need him: and he that is a blessing, shall be blessed; the Lord God shall bless him with an increase of his substance, who hath most emptied himself for him, and his. Its true that the SOULsoul of the liberal properly taken, shall be a gainer by his liberality: no more thriving Christians, then the merciful Christians, what they expend in temporals is abundantly returned in spirituals. But because there is so much of carnal, even in too many Christians, and have need of encouragements suited to our tempers, therefore to our spiritual advantages, which are the greatest these outward encouragements are added as often most taking with our too carnal hearts. So that this is the sense of the place. The liberal man, as the reward and encouragement of his liberality, shall prosper in the world. And as it follows, Hehe that watereth, the soul of the needy, his waters shall not fail, but he shall be watered also himself. God will give in to him, according as he hath given out to others.

And for their farther encouragement, saith the wiseman, Pro. 19. 17. Hehe that hath pity on the poor, lendeth unto the Lord, and that which he hath given, shall he pay him again. Ifif that which thou givest be repaid thee again, how can it be said to be lost? Indeed the poor, unto whom thou givest, are not able to repay thee again, yet having such an alsufficient Suretysurety, as God himself, who hath undertaken the repayment, thou need'st not doubt thereof. Oh happy is that man that becomes a Creditorcreditor to his Creatour, and makes God his debtor! whoseWhose is the earth, and the fulness thereof. Heaven and earth shall be emptied before he shall want a royal payment.

Fear not to be an Vsurerusurer, so thou lendest unto God, make him
thy debtor, and he will surely pay thee Principalprincipal and Interestinterest. Allow him his time (for that he will have) and he will not only pay the debt, but allow thee for the forbearance. The ungodly borroweth, and payeth not again: but this shall never be said of the righteous God: Hehe is just, and will make good payment of whatsoever is lent unto him.

It is true, the Lord loves to deal upon trust, and uses to make payment by way of Returnsreturns. Hehe will be trusted, and those that will not give him Creditcredit, let them if they can, put their estates into surer hands. And he uses to pay by the way of Returus, it may be neither in the same kind, nor in the same Countrycountry. Sometimes tis so that he pays not in the same kind, bread for bread, or clothes for clothes, or money or money, Nornor possibly may he make his payment in this forreign land, where thou art a Merchantmerchant adventurer, but may give thee his bill of exchange to receive it in thine own country, that better Countrycountry, which is thy home, and inheritance, which shall be the reward of thy works, and labour of love, which thou shewestshowest to his name. And if he do thus, does he thee any wrong? Is it not best for thee that thou receive thy goods at thy home? Is it any harm to thee to receive Silversilver for thy Brassbrass, Goldgold for thy Silversilver, Rubiesrubies for thy Goldgold, a treasure in Heavenheaven, for thy treasure on Earthearth? Doubt not that he will be behind hand with thee: yet stick not if thou shouldst be put to it, to wait for payment in full till hereafter: and for the present this thou may'st depend upon from Pro. 28. 27. He that giveth to the poor shall not lack, he shall have in hand whats needful at least. Hehe shall not lack and there may be more in this word, then if he had said, I will presently pay thee all: Forfor all that thou hast, if thou shouldst hold it never so close, cannot secure thee from ever coming to want; as great as thy abundance is, thou maist come to want before thou diest. But what thy abundance cannot do, this promise of God can and doth for thee even give thee security that thou shalt never lack.

Again Eccl. 11. 1. Cast thy bread vponupon the waters, for thou shalt find it after many days. Byby bread is here meant all things necessary for the support of mens lives. And by casting their bread upon the waters, is meant their giving freely of that which they have for the relief of the poor, whose watry eyes bewray their great necessity. And though that which thou bestowest on them, may seem to
be as clearly lost and cast away, as that which is thrown down the Riverriver, or cast into the Seasea, where ther is no likel • ihood of receiving it again, because given to those who can no way recompencerecompense thee; whence arose that Greek Proverbproverb

Thouthou sowest upon the water, which is usually applyed to such as bestow kindnesses where they are utterly lost.

Yetyet thou shalt find it after many days, Lavater in locum saith, that here is implyed a promise of long life to the charitable, that God will lengthen out his days to a good old age. Though this falls out true in many, yet I conceive it not to be here intended, nor to be the meaning of the words, but rather, this, that though thy reward doth not presently appear, yet if thou bestowest thine alms with a sincere heart, it shall not be lost, but certainly be returned into thy bosomebosom with increase.

Yet further saith the Lord by the Prophetprophet Isa. 58. 7, 8. &etcc. If thou deal thy bread to the hungry, and bring the poor that are cast out, to thy house, and when thou seest the naked, if thou cover him, and that thou hide not thy self from thine own flesh, by tnrning thy sacesac from him; Thenthen (see what a gracious promise of signal blessings follow hereupon) shall thy light break forth as the Morningmorning, that is, then shall the night of thine adversity be dispelled, and the day spring of thy prosperity break forth as the Morningmorning-light: and thy righteousness shall go before thee, that is, the fruit and reward of thy charity shall be visible to all: the glory of the Lord shall be thy rereward, that is, the God of glory shall by his power and providence both go before thee, and follow thee with his blessing. And verse 10. Ifif thou draw out thy soul to the hungry, and Satisfiesatisfy the afflicted soul, that is, afford that hearty relief unto him, which shall satisfiesatisfy his necessity, then shall thy light rise in obscurity, thy adversity shall be turned into prosperity, Andand the Lord shall guide thee continually, and satisfiesatisfy thy soul in drought, as thou didst satisfiesatisfy the poor mans soul by supplying his wants, so the Lord will supply thee with a sufficiency in the greatest dearth and famine; and make fat thy bones; and thou shalt be as a watered garden, and a little spring of water, whose waters fail not; an emblem of a flourishing, and prosperous estate, which doth usually follow, and accompany merciful men.

Yea our blessed Saviour, Math. 19. 29. promisethPromiseth, that such as for his sake shall this or any other way part with their estates, or
any part or portions of them, shall receive an hundred fold here, and inherit eternal life hereafter: here in this life he shall have the return of an hundred fold, which many Christians have found true in their own experience, and with thankfulness to God have acknowledged as much.

And what variety of expressions doth our Saviour use in Luke 6. 38. toTo assure us of a large reward here of all our labour of love shewedshowed to his Ministersministers, and members? Givegive, saith he, and it shall be gien to you again, good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over. Forfor your encouragement unto this duty of giving to the poor, Ourour Saviour first annexeth a general promise of return, Givegive, and it shall be given to you again, where he giveth you a Billbill of his hand, that you shall be no looser by what you give to his poor, but shall be repay'd, and that with advantage, as the following words declare, you shall have good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over, we account it good measure, when it is heaped up, but when it is not only heaped up, but pressed down, that is more; but when it is heaped up, pressed down; and then heaped up, and running over again, who can but say, that this is good measure indeed? Yet thus God dealesdeals with merciful men, they shall have mercies and blessings heaped up, pressed down, and running over. Howhow truely then may I take up the words of the Psalmistpsalmist, Blessed is he that considereth the poor; Hehe shall not only be blessed, but he shall have blessings heaped up, and running over! which the Apostle St. Paul expresseth very Emphatically by the similitude of reaping and sowing, 2 Cor. 9. 6. Hehe that soweth sparingly, shall reap sparingly, but he which soweth bountifully, shall reap bountifully. Asas men sow, so shall they reap, the more liberally they give to good uses, the more bountifully they shall receive from God: they shall find a plentifullplentiful harvest, as the fruit of all their cost and pains. Dr. Hammond in his practical Catechismcatechism, quoting these words of the Apostle Hehe that soweth bountifully, shall reap bountifully, addeth this gloss, Byby reaping bountifully, I conceive is meant, not onelyonly Gods abundant retributions of glory in another world, but even his payments of temporal plenty, and blessings here to those who have been willing to make that Christian VseUse of that earthly talent commited to their Stewardingstewarding.

div.p: Though these proofesproofs of Scripture are sufficient to convince any Christian of the truth of the Doctrinedoctrine, yet for your farther Satisfactionsatisfaction, I shall briefly give you the Judgmentjudgment both of some ancient Fathersfathers, and modern Divinesdivines concerning the same.

p.q:
The Authorauthor of the whole Dutyduty of man, treating of Almsalms in Partitionpartition 17. saithSaith, Therethere is but one Objectionobjection to be made against a cheerful giving of Almsalms, and that is, Thethe danger of impoverishing ones self by what one gives. Toto which he answers in these words; that this is sure a vain supposition, God having particularly promised the contrary to the charitable: Thatthat it shall bring blessings on them, even in these outward things. The liberal soul shall be made fat, & he that watereth, shall be watered also himself, Pro. 11. 25. Hehe that giveth to the poor, shall not lack, Pro. 28. 27. And many the like texts ther are, so that one may truly say, Thisthis Objectionobjection is grounded in direct unbelief. The short of it is, we dare not trust God,
for this giving to the poor, is directly Thethe putting our wealth into his hands: Hehe that giveth to the poor, lendeth unto the Lord, Pro. 19. 17. andAnd that too, on solemn promise of repayment, as it follows in that verse, Thatthat which he hath given will he pay him again. Itit is amongst men thought a great disparagment, when we refuse to trust them: it shewsshows, we either think them not sufficient or not honest. How vile an affront is it then to God, thus to distrust him? Nay indeed, how horrid blasphemy, to doubt the security of that, for which he has thus expreslyexpressly past his word, who is the Lord of all, and therefore cannot be insufficient: and who is the God of truth, and therefore will not fail to make good his promise?

Let not then that infidel-fear of future-want contract and shut up thy bowels from thy poor brother: for though he be never like to pay, yet God becomes his Suretysurety, and enters bond with him, and will most assuredly pay thee with increase.

Therefore it is so far from being damage to thee, Thusthus to give, that it is thy great advantage. Anyany man would rather chusechoose to put his money in some sure hand, where he may both improve, and be certain of it at his need, than to let it lye unprofitable by him, especially if he be in danger of thieves, or other accidents, by which he may probably lose it: Nownow alassalas! allAll that we possess is in emminent-danger of losing: innumerable accidents there are, which may in an instant bring a rich man to beggery; he that doubts this, let him but read the story of IobJob, and he will there find an example of it. And therefore what so prudent course can we take for our wealth, as to put it out of the reach of those accidents, by thus lending it to God, where we may be sure to find it ready at our greatest need, and that too with improvment and increase? In which respect it is, that the Apostle compares almesalms to Seedseed 2 Cor. 9. 10. We know it is the nature of Seedseed that is sowen, to multiply and increase; and so do all our acts of Mercymercy, they return not single, and naked to us, but bring in their sheaves with them, a most plenteous and bountiful harvest. God dealesdeals not with our almesalms, as we too often do with his graces, wrap them up in a napkin, so that they shall never bring in any advantage to us, but makes us most rich Returnsreturns. And therefore we have all reason, most cheerfully, yea-joyfully, to set to this duty, which we have such invitations to, as well in respect of our own Interestinterest, as our Neighborsneighbors needs.

div.p: Thus have you the truth of the point proved both by divine, and humane testimonies. I should now proceed to give you some instances for the farther confirmation thereof. But I must beseech you first to take these two Cautionscautions.

1. Notnot to ascribe the reward to any merit of your good works, but only to the free grace, and rich mercy of God. Itit is his rich mercy, that we have wherewithallwherewithal to give, and his free grace, that we have an heart to give, and his abundant goodness, that he accepteth our works of charity, and rewardeth them with all sorts of blessings, both temporal, Spiritualspiritual and eternal; but we cannot merit any thing at his hand; by giving him that which is his own.

2. Thoughthough our Almsalms-deeds are sacrifices acceptable and welpleasing unto God through Christ; and though he hath bound himself by many gracious promises to reward the same both here, and hereafter: yet far be it from us to perform them meerly out of hope of reward, but rather for conscience-sake, in obedience to the command of God, (who hath required them at our hands,) and in testimony of our thankfulness unto him, for what he hath graciously bestowed on us. As we are commanded to obey the Magistratemagistrate, not so much for fear of punishment, and hope of reward, as for conscience-sake, in obedience to the command of God, Rom. 13. 5. So ought we to distribute our Almsalms not so much for the reward-sake, as out of conscience, for the Lords-sake.

I deny not but Christians in their well-doing may for their encouragement have respect to the recompencerecompense of reward, but not onelyonly, and chiefly. Thethe chief and principal Endsends we should aim at in all our good works, are, Thethe glory of God, Andand Obedienceobedience to his command. Ourour respect to the recompencerecompense of reward ought to be subordinate unto these. The truth is, Thisthis temporal reward should not so much be looked on, as an argument to perswadepersuade us to give, but as an answer of an Objectionobjection against Givinggiving. Thou wilt be ready to say, I may want it my self, or mine may want it. But do but believe, that God will repay thee, and with overplus; and then that doubt willbe taken out of the way.

These two Cautionscautions premised, I shall proceed in the confirmation of the point from the examples of many charitable persons, who have in temporal mercies been abundantly recompensed for the kindness they have shewedshowed to the Ministersministers and Membersmembers of Christ.

The widdow of Sareptah nourished the Prophetprophet Elijah in her house during the whole time of famine: and how did the Lord abundantly recompense this her charity, by his miraculous preserving and encreasing her meal and oyl, whereby her family was nourished. As also by restori • ng her Son to life again, after his Soulsoul was departed? 1 King 17. 22. And by causing the Prophetprophet to continue with her many Monethsmonths, to feed her soul with spiritual, as she had his body, with carnal food.

How abundantly was the Shunamite's kindness to the Prophetprophet Elisha, recompensed?
1. By the gift of a Son after long barrenness.
2. By restoring her Son to life again when he was dead. 2 King. 16.
3. By forewarning her of a famine approaching, 2 King. 8. 1, 4.
4. By the restoring of her house and land, lost in her long absence; by reason of the famine, 2 King. 4. 28.

Notable is the instance of IobJob. Whatwhat a merciful man he was, we may read chap. 29. 12, 13, 15. I delivered the poor that cryed, and the fatherless, and him that had none to help him. The blessing of him that was ready to perish came upon me, and I caused the widdows heart to sing for joy. I was eyes to the blind, and feet I was to the lame, I was a father to the poor. Andand chap. 31. 16, & 22▪ Ifif I have withheld the poor from their desire or have caused the eyes of the widdow to fail, or have eaten my morsel alone, and the fatherless hath not eaten thereof; Ifif I have seen any perish for want of cloathing, or any poor without covering; Ifif his loyns have not blessed me, and if he were not warmed with the fleece of my sheep: Thenthen let mine arms fall from my shoulder-blade, and mine arm be broken from the bone. I have transcribed his own words thus at large, that I might set this worthy pattern before the readers eyes.

But you will say, what became of this merciful man? didDid he prosper? didDid he flourish, and grow great? whoWho so poor as poor IobJob after all these acts of mercy? How long after was it, that we find this merciful man a miserable man, strip'd naked of all that ever he had? But, Firstfirst, Itit was not his own mercy, but Sathans malice that brought him down: Itit was the Devildevil that set the Sabeans, and Chaldeans, upon him, to plunder, and carry away all that he had. And Secondly, what became of IobJob afterwards, after Sathan had done his worst? youYou may read, chap. 42. 10. &etcc. Thatthat the Lord turned
the Captivitycaptivity of Job and gave him twice so much as he had before, and blessed his latter end more than his beginning, so he had fourteen thousand sheep, and Sixsix thousand Camelscamels: a thousand yoke of Oxenoxen, and a thousand sheeshe asses: Hehe had also seven Sonssons, and three daughters.

We read how Publius the chief man of the Islandisland of Melita (into which St. Paul, & many others with him were cast by Shipwrack) received and lodged them three days courteously: and in the next verse we read how the father of Publius, when he lay desperately sick of a feaver, and bloody-flux, was recovered by St. Paul, and restored to his former health. To these Examplesexamples, recorded in Scripture, I shall add a few more out of ancient, and modern writings.

div.p: The story of Tiberius the second is pertinent to this purpose, which take in the words of that Reverendreverend person before-mentioned in his Sermonsermon at the Spittle. This Tiberius was very famous for his bounty to the poor, insomuch that his wife was wont to blame him for it, and speaking to him once, how he wasted his treasure that way, he told her. Hehe should never want money, so long as in Obedienceobedience to Christs Commandcommand he did supply the necessities of the poor. Andand presently see how providence ordered it! Immediately after he had given much this way, under a marble table which was taken up, he found a great treasure, and news was brought him too of the death of one Narses, a very rich man, who had given his whole Estateestate unto him.

Famous is the story of that charitable Bishopbishop of Millain, who as he was travelling with his Servantservant, overtook some poor people who begged an alms of him: wherupon he asked his man what money he had about him, who answered Three crowns, which he commanded him to give unto them: but the servant thinking himself wiser than his Mastermaster, gave them but two crowns, not knowing what occasions they might have for money before that got home. Not long after Somesome Noblemennoblemen meeting the Bishopbishop, and knowing him to be a very charitable man, appointed two hundred Crownscrowns to be paid to the Bishopsbishops Servantservant for his Mastersmasters use. The Servantservant
having received the money, presently with great joy acquainted his Mastermaster therewith, whereupon said the Bishopbishop, Thouthou mayst now see how in wronging the poor of their due, by keeping back the third crown which I intended them, thou hast likewise wronged me, Si enimtres dedisses, trecentos accepisses &etcc. If thou hadst given those three Crownscrowns I commanded thee to give, thou hadst received three hundred Crownscrowns whereas now I have but two. Melanc. apudApud IohJoh. Manlium in Loc. Com.

It is recorded of Mary the wife of Alexander Fa • rnese, Prince of Parma, that being childless, she conceived an hope, that if she would take into her house some Orphan, or poor mans child, and there train him up, God would bestow a Son upon her. Whereupon she took a poor mans Son into her care, and gave order for his education and according to her expectation, at nine Monethsmonths end she was delivered of a Son.
