That though I cast my bread upon the waters where it may seem to be lost. yet I shall find it after many days, it shall certainly be returned into my bosomebosom with increase? And hath my Saviour for my encouragement promised, Luk. 6. 36. Thatthat if I give unto the poor, it shall be given to me again, good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, running over? Thenthen certainly, there is no such compendious way to thrive and prosper in the world, as by my liberality to the poor.

2. Prefer Heavenheaven and the things thereof before this earth, and earthly things. Thoughthough the temporal reward which I have so much insisted on, be a great encouragement, yet the greatest encouragement is the spiritual and eternal reward that the Lord hath promised. And that this may be the more prevailing encouragement, learn to esteem and prize things spiritual and eternal above all things that are but temporal. Supposesuppose it should so fall out, that you should never receive in kind what you bestow, yet count those temporal things put off at the best rate, which you receive in things spiritual and eternal. Valuevalue grace and glory above all the treasures of the earth, and count your selves to grow rich men, according to your abounding in grace, and your evidences for glory. And esteem it an unthristy Savingsaving, and holding in, where you have an opportunity to improve in your inner man by expending of your outward substance.

Till Heavenheaven be valued above earth, this great Argumentargument encouraging to Acts of bounty and mercy will lose its efficacy. When God says, Cast thy bread upon the waters, for thou shalt find it again after many dayesdays; the Worldlingworldling will be ready to demand. But how shall I find it? inIn what way shall it be returned me? Shall I have bread for bread, or money for my bread. or houses or Landslands for my money? probably thou may'st. But suppose not so, yet it shall be better than so, thou shalt have in grace what thou partest with in bread or money; thou shalt reap in Heavenheaven, what thou sowest on the waters.

I but the worlding will reply; I do not mean to part with my bread, or my money so. Nono, I know thou dost not; but the reason is, because thou lovestlouest this earth more than Heavenheaven. Thou sayest, Willwill Grace feed me? Will Grace cloath me? Can I keep my self, and my Familyfamily? Can we live and be maintained, and preserved from poverty and beggery here, by hopes of glory hereafter?

Go fool, and learn better what God is, and what his everlasting mercy is; let the lasting treasures, the durable riches be more priz'd and valued by thee, and this will stop thy mouth, and silence thine heart from such vain reasonings. Thou wilt never again say, I cannot spare my bread, or my money, when by spending it for God thou seest thou makest him thy debter, who will pay it thee again in spiritual and eternal good things, if once thou account these to be better than thy bread, or thy money.

But till thou art come to be settled in this Judgementjudgement, and belief, both that the good things of God are infinitely better than the good things of this earth; and that what thou sowest in the earth, thou shalt certainly reap in Heavenheaven; till thou comest in good earnest to be of this mind, God's poor are like to be but little the better for thee.

'Tis this, beloved, that will effectually do it, will open your hearts, and open your hands in bounty and liberality for God, when you come to be rooted in the practical belief of this principle, upon which the practice of all Religionreligion stands, and is upheld in the world; Thatthat Heavenheaven is better than Earthearth: if this other be added to it, Thatthat what is sincerely laid out for God in the Earthearth, shall certainly be repayed in Heavenheaven; besides that return which the Lord here in this world oftentimes makes to the charitable.
2. For the Meansmeans tending to help you for the better managing of it; take these following.
1. Either follow the Exampleexample of the Primitiveprimitive Saintssaints, in setting apart something every Lords Dayday out of the former weeks gettings.
Or, 2. Devote unto God a certain portion of thy yearly incomes for charitable uses.

That the former way of setting apart something every Lords Dayday for the relief of the poor, was the practice of the Primitiveprimitive Christians, is clear from that of the Apostle to the Corinthians, 1 Cor. 16. 1, 2. Nownow concerning the Collectioncollection for the Saintssaints, as I have given order to the Churcheschurches of Galatia, even so do ye. VponUpon the first
day of the week (which is the Lords Dayday) let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him. Thisthis way and course concerns such in special who live upon their daily labours.

But to such Gentlemengentlemen, and others who live upon their Rentsrents and Officesoffices; and to such Merchantsmerchants and Citizenscitizens who once a year cast up their accounts, I would commend the latter way of devoting unto God a certain portion of their yearly income by Rentrent or otherwise, and then separating it from the rest, to account it a sacred stock for the poor, not to be imployedemployed to any other use.

All men naturally (through the corruption that is in them) are hard-hearted, and close-handed, very unwilling to part with any thing considerable upon sudden occasions for charitable uses. But having aforehand set apart something, their ears, hearts and hands, are open to every charitable motion, and very ready and forward are they the more liberally to contribute thereunto of what is laid by; rejoycing that they have met with so good an object of Charitycharity.

As for the quota pars, what proportion every one ought to set apart out of his yearly income for good uses, I do not find it particularly set down in the Wordword of God, and therefore dare not positively determine the same: and the rather, because there are so many circumstances which alter the case, that no certain rule can be given, but shall leave it to the discretion and ingenuity of the prudent Christian.

But though the Scripture doth not determine the exact proportion to be set apart for good works, yet doth it command us, to give out proportionably to what God hath given unto us; to open our hands wide to the necessities of the poor; to be rich in good works, and the like. Yea the Scripture doth commend unto us the examples of very bountiful Christians, as of Dorcas, who is said to be full of good works, and alms-deeds which she did, Actact. 9. 36. And of Cornelius, who is said to give much alms, Actact. 10. 2. And of the Macedonians, who are said, to give to their power, yea and beyond their power, 2 Cor. 8. 3. It likewse commendeth unto us the example of IacobJacob, who in testimony of his thankfulness unto God for what he should bestow upon him, vowed the tenth thereof unto God, for pious and charitable uses; as Gen. 28. 20, 22. And Jacob vowed a vow unto God, saying, Ofof all that thou shalt give me, I will surely give the tenth unto thee.

These examples are left upon record for our imitation; for as the Apostle speaketh, Rom. 15. 4. Whatsoever things were written aforetime, were written for our learning, and for our admonition. Thethe most that I have heard or read of, who have taken this course, to cons • ecrate unto God a certain portion of their estate to charitable uses, have followed the example of IacobJacob, in giving a tenth part unto God. And as God did exceedingly bless IacobJacob after his vow; so hath he likewise blessed very many others, after their like vow unto God.

Mr. Stock in his funeral Sermonsermon at the burial of the Lord Harrington, speaking of his Charitycharity, declared that in his life time, he gave the tenth part of his yearly revenue to the poor. Mr. Gataker in his funeral Sermonsermon at the burial of Mr. IohnJohn Parker Merchantmerchant, and Citizencitizen of London, speaking of his Charitycharity, saith, Thatthat at his first effectual Callcall, among other things he then resolved upon, this was one, to set apart every year a tenth of his gain for the relief of the poor and needy; and that God from that time abundantly advanced his estate. Andand questionless, if such Merchantsmerchants, who usually ensure their goods upon their apprehension of danger at Seasea, would sincerely promise unto God, in testimony of their thankfulness unto him, the tenth of what should come safe into their hands, they might receive far greater returns than they do.

In the Lifelife of Dr. Hammond, written by Dr. Fell, I find this expression,
Thethe rate and summ of what the Doctordoctor devoted, was the tenth of all his income, wherein he was so strictly punctual, that commonly the first thing he did was to compute, and separate the poor mans share. Andand how his stock increased notwithstanding his abundant giving out to the relief of others, the history at large declareth. The like I read in the Lifelife of Mr. William Wheatly, Ministerminister of Banbury, how for many years he set apart the tenth of his yearly comings in, both out of his Temporal and Ecclesiastical Meansmeans, and that his Estateestate prospered the better after he took that course. Toto these I could add many more out of the Liveslives of good and charitable men, and out of several funeral Sermonssermons, which are printed and published. And could name multitudes of men now living, who have devoted the like, and greater portion out of their estates for charitable uses, and are ready to attest the truth of this discourse, Thatthat they are no losers, but great gainers in Temporals by what they have given to the poor.

Mr. Richard Baxter in his Learnedlearned and Usefulluseful Piecepiece, called A Christian Directorydirectory, Partpart the 4th. fol. 195. ofOf the quotapars, what proportion is meet for most men to devote for charitable uses, whether the tenth part of their increase be not ordinarily a fit proportion? hathHath this expression,

p.q: Though the proportion of the tenth part is too much for some, and much too little for others, yet for the most part, I think it as likely a proportion as it is fit for another to prescribe in particular.

div.p: Yet I would not be thought to impose this as a proportion to be observed by all; for all mens hearts are not alike inlargedenlarged with love and bounty: and some there are who have no more than is necessary for the comfortable support of themselves and family; from whom less is required for the relief of others. But I would advise such whom the Lord hath blessed with a plentiful estate, so that their necessary expencesexpenses are, or might be, far less than their incomes, to devote a tenth part of their whole yearly income to charitable uses: I say, of their whole yearly income, without first deducting any part thereof for diet, cloaths, or other necessary expencesexpenses; for the tenth of the remainder will be a very inconsiderable proportion for a rich man to devote to Charitycharity, and far short of that which the Scripture seemeth to call for.

And know assuredly, that this course is so far from being a means of diminishing your stock and store, that if it be managed as it ought, according to the forementioned rules and directions, it is the surest and safest means, the most compendious course of increasing it, through the secret blessing of God, which accompanieth the same; which hath been sufficiently demonstrated in the foregoing discourse.

2. Be careful on whom thou bestowest thine alms; for by giving to such common beggars who are able to work, and yet are so lazy, that they will not work, but would live by the sweat of other mens brows; I say, by relieving such, we shall both maintain them in their idle and wicked life; and they who are truly poor, and ought to be looked upon as the proper objects of our Charitycharity, will be neglected, or at least scanted of that, which of right belongeth to them.

I am not against the relieving of all beggars; some of them I know are blind, others lame, aged, and past their work; these impotent poor, in regard of their present condition, are objects of Charitycharity, but not the impudent poor, who have strength enough to work, and will not, those canting vagrants, who are the burthen of the earth,
and shame of the Kingdomkingdom, for these I have no charity: Neitherneither had the Apostle St. Paul, who towards God's poor was full of compassion; but for the Devil's poor, he gave this command, 2 Thes. 3. 10. Thatthat if any would not work, neither should he eat; that hunger and necessity might drive them to labour. Erasmus mentions a kind of mercy meetest for such, 'tis misericordia puniens: Surelysurely the Whip is more their due, than food: Bridewell to entertain them, than an Almsalms-house.

III. Anotheranother Meansmeans for the attaining this grace of Christian Charitycharity, is this, Be earnest with God in prayer, that he would be pleased to bestow upon thee that adorning and enriching grace of Charitycharity, and accept thy offering. Thisthis Sacrificesacrifice, as it must be offered up to Heavenheaven; so it must be fetched from Heavenheaven. The gift of a merciful and charitable heart, is one of those gifts that come down from above, even the Father of Lightslights, Iam. 1. 17. If thou receivest not this gift from God, thy poor Brotherbrother is like to have no gift from thee. Now it must be thy prayer that must fetch down this gift from God. Lift up thine heart to the Lord, and beg a merciful and compassionate soul; beg of God that he would make thee ready to every good work, willing to communicate to the poor members of Christ, according to thine ability, and their necessity, that thereby thou mayest lay up in store for thy self a good foundation against the time to come, and so lay hold on eternal life: pray for a willing heart, and pray for acceptance of thy gift, that thine alms may be such a sacrifice, and so offered up, that therewith the Lord may be well pleased.

Having thus shewedshowed you the Meansmeans on our part to be performed for attaining and exercising this grace of Charitycharity: I shall close this discourse with answering two or three Objectionsobjections.
Object. 1. Some object the greatness of their charge, the number of their children, who must be cared for, and thereupon have little to give to the poor.

Answ. 1. Hasthast thou many children, thou oughtest the rather to be charitable, that thereby thou mayest entail God's blessing upon them, which is the best portion, and surest inheritance thou canst leave them; that will secure their stock, and improve their store; whereas unmercifulness to the poor will intail a curse instead of a blessing upon the persons and estates of thy children.

2. Thou who objectest the number of thy children as a plea for thy
parsimony, how justly may God then lessen the number, and so take away this excuse, by taking thy children from thee.

3. Supposesuppose thou hast many children, it may be half a score, reckon God for one more; give unto him a childs portion; I mean, bestow upon the poor, for his sake, as much every year, as one child stands thee in; give unto them a childs portion, and I dare boldly say, thou wilt not be the poorer, but rather a great gainer. For thereby wilt thou procure God's blessing upon thy self and children, which in truth is all in all; and without which, all is like to come to nothing, as weewe see by daily experience; which made St. Austin say, Haeredi praestabis, quicquid misericordiae causa de ejus portioneportion detraxeris, Aug. deDe Tempore, Serm. 76. That which thou givest out of thine estate to charitable uses, will be no loss to thy children, but rather a great advantage. Yea the Spirit of God in setting forth the happiness of a merciful man, saith, Hishis children shall fare the better for his goodness and bounty, as Psal. 37. 16. He is ever merciful, and lendeth, and his seed is blessed; that is, God will bless his children, not only with spiritual, but also with temporal blessings.
2. ObjObi. Manymany Professorsprofessors in these daiesdays are very barren in good works.

Answ. Fruitless and uncharitable Christians may make a profession of Religionreligion, but questionless they are no sound Christians, nor sincere Professorsprofessors. Forfor most certain it is, that the Electelect of God do put on bowels of mercy and compassion, as the Apostle speaketh, Col. 3. 12. And therefore an uncharitable Christian is a meer contradiction. For who is a Christian but he who conforms himself to the Lawlaw and Lifelife of Christ? The substance of whose Lawlaw is Charitycharity, and whose Lifelife was spent in going about doing good, some way or other, to the soul and bodies of men and women.

Whosoever therefore having this worlds goods, seeth his Brotherbrother in need, and shuttethshuteth up his bowels of compassion from him, and will not communicate any thing considerable towards his necessities; let his profession be never so specious and glorious in the eyes of men, yet certainly he is but a rotten Professorprofessor, and dissembling Hypocritehypocrite in the sight of God. In Matth. 25. 23. We find that liberality to the members of Christ is made the special touchstone of true Faithfaith and Godlinessgodliness. For they are the charitable persons, who at the great day of Judgmentjudgment will appear to be the Sheepsheep at Christs right hand, and shall hear that joyful sentence of absolution,
Comecome ye blessed of my Father, inherit the Kingdomkingdom prepared for you, from the foundation of the world: for I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in: I was naked, and ye cloathedclothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me.

And on the other side, all unmerciful men, who have not relieved Christ in his members, whatsoever profession of Religionreligion they have made here in this world; yet at the last day will appear to be the Goats set on Christs left hand, and shall hear that dreadful sentence of condemnation, Depart from me ye cursed into everlasting fire, prepared for the Devildevil and his Angelsangels: Forfor I was an hungred, and ye gave me no meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me no drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me not in: naked, and ye cloathedclothed me not: sick and in prison, and ye visited me not. Hencehence it appeareth, that as mercy and bounty to the poor members of Christ, is a conspicuous evidence of true Faithfaith, and sincere godliness in a Christian, and signally declare him pious: so illiberality, and unmercifulness to them, is a clear mark of infidelity, and ungodliness, and signally declare him as an unbeliever; so a wicked and prophaneprofane person: Thereforetherefore I should much question the sincerity of their faith and piety, who making a profession of Religionreligion, shewshow little or no charity to the poor members of Christ. For as the Apostle IamesJames speaketh, c. 1. v. 21. Pure Religionreligion and undefield before God, and the Father, is this, to visit the fatherless and widdows in their affliction: Implyingimplying, that works of mercy and charity rightly performed, are clear evidences of the truth of our Religionreligion, and of the sincerity of our Professionprofession. And if you look into the Scriptures, you shall scarce read of a man truly godly, but you may read also, that he was merciful and charitable, forward to every good work.
So much shall suffice for this Pointpoint of Doctrinedoctrine.
A word or two for my Brethrens sake of the first Doctrinedoctrine raised from the foregoing verse, which is the principal Pointpoint there intended by our Saviour, which was this.
17. That all needfullneedful succour, and good entertainment ought to be afforded in special to the Ministersministers of the Gospel.

Our Saviour in commending objects to our Charitycharity, in the first place mentioneth Prophetsprophets, and the Righteousrighteous ones, saying, Hehe that receiveth a Prophetprophet in the name of a Prophetprophet, shall receive a Prophet's reward; and then addeth, Hehe that receiveth a Righteousrighteous man in the name of a Righteousrighteous man, &etcc.

Indeed, so general must be the extent and emanation of our Charitycharity, that it must not exclude any who are in want and distress. For though we may, and ought to put a difference between men upon whom we bestow our Charitycharity; yet ought we not to restrain it from any men who are in want; but must act the grace of Charitycharity towards them who have not the grace of Faithfaith. Yeayea, we ought to do good unto all, as the Apostle exhorteth, Gal. 6. 13. But especially unto them who are of the housholdhousehold of Faithfaith. Andand among them chiefly to the Ministersministers of Christ. Soso as this object of Charitycharity, Prophetprophet, is not here to be taken exclusively, but by way of eminency and preferment: Ministersministers are before, and above others, with more readiness and chearfulness to be ministredministered unto.

The people of Israel we read were commanded once and again not to leave nor forsake their Levites, especially when they were reduced into any streights and exegencies, as Deut. 12. 19. andAnd 14. 27. Then much less should the Ministersministers of the Gospel be left and forsaken by the people of God, when they lye under any want or distress.

The examples of God's people that have gone before us in the performance of this duty are many, both in the Oldold and Newnew Testament. It is recorded to the perpetual praise and commendation of Obadiah, that he hid the Prophetsprophets of God by fifty in a cave from the cruelty of IezabelJezebel, and sustained them with food, and ministredministered all things necessary unto them, 1 King. 18. 13. We read likewise how the widdow of Sarephath nourished the Prophetprophet Elijah in her house for many dayesdays and years, even so long as the famin continued, 1 King. 17. 15, 16. The kindness of the good Shunamite to the Prophetprophet Elisha, is largely reproved, 2 King. 4. 8, &etcc. Itit fell
on a day that Elisha passed to Shunem, where was a great woman, and she constrained him to eat bread; that is, to refresh himself with food. Andand so it was, that as oft as he passed by, he turned in thither to eat bread. Havinghaving found good entertainment, and hearty welcome, he did the oftner visit the family. Andand she said unto her Husbandhusband, Beholdbehold now I perceive, that this is an holy man of God, which passeth by us continually, let us make a little chamber, I pray thee, on the wall, and let us set for him there a bed, and a table, and a stool, and a candlestick. Underunder these, other necessary accommodations are comprized. The good woman desired of her Husbandhusband, that a chamber might be made for the Prophetprophet on the wall; perhaps not that she wanted room in her house to lodge him in, but because she considered, that the noise of a great family might be some disturbance to the Prophet's study and devotion; therefore thought it convenient to provide such a chamber for him, where he might be more retired, and have the free ingress and egress; that by those accommodations he might be encouraged the oftner to take up his lodging there.

Rom. 16. 2. It is set down as the height and crown of Phebe's good works, that she had been a succourer of the Apostle Paul in his wants and straits. Andand in 2 Tim. 1. 16. weWe read how Onesiphorus refreshed and relieved the Apostle in his suffering condition, and was not ashamed of his chain; that is, though he were a prisoner, and under restraint for the Gospelsgospels sake, yet Onesiphorus owned him, shewedshowed him all respect, succoured and relieved him in that his low condition. Gaius likewise, a godly, wealthy Citizencitizen of Corinth, is famous for that kind entertainment and succour which he gave to the Apostle, and the Churchchurch with him, Rom. 16. 23.

It is recorded to the commendation of King Edward the sixth, that he afforded all needful succour, and good entertainment to Bucer, Fagius, and other Divinesdivines, when they fled into this Kingdomkingdom by reason of the troubles in their own Nationnation. And Beza in his Epistleepistle ad Regem IacobumJacobum, maketh an honourable mention of a liberal collection of the Churchchurch of Scotland sent to the French-Ministersministers, who were banished Religionis causa.

Here are fair Copiescopies for us to write after. And indeed why are these things written, and left upon record to posterity, but for our learning? Not so much for our admiration, as for our imitation, that we might follow their steps, and write after their copy; which
St. Paul testifies of the Macedonians, 2 Cor. 9. 2. How that very many of them were stirred up and provoked to a liberal contribution to the poor Saintssaints at Jerusalem by the forwardness and zeal of the Corinthians. And St. Austin (Confes. libLib. 9. cap. 2.) confesseth, that the examples of God's servants, did burn and consume his own lukewarmness; and their fervent zeal set an edge on his Devotiondevotion.
To these Examplesexamples I shall add a few REASONSreasons for the better enforcing this duty upon you.

Reas. I. Because Ministersministers being supported, are like to be most serviceable to the Churchchurch of God. Theythey are Spiritualspiritual Fathersfathers, to beget men unto Christ. They are his Anbassadou • rs, and stand in his stead to reveal the Mysteriesmysteries of the Kingdomkingdom, sent forth to be reconcilers betwixt God and this sinful world; to pray and beseech them to be reconciled unto God, 2 Cor. 5 20. Their work is to bear the Namename of God, to publish the salvation of God before the world; to open the eyes of the blind, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins, and an inheritance among them that are sanctified: Inin which respect Ministersministers of the Gospel are more useful and serviceable in their generation, than either Lawyers, Physiciansphysicians or Tradesmentradesmen, which yet are useful enough.
1. Lawyers indeed may be a means of settling your Rightright in your Goodsgoods and Landslands: Butbut Ministersministers of settling your Rightright to your heavenly Inheritanceinheritance.
2. Physiciansphysicians may cure the maladies of your bodies: Butbut Ministersministers are sent to cure the diseases of your souls.

3. Merchantsmerchants, and all sorts of Tradesmentradesmen may replenish a Landland with all manner of Commoditiescommodities necessary for this life: Butbut Ministersministers only bring in such heavenly and spiritual treasures as spring up into the everlasting treasure.

So that by supplying their bodily wants, you do comfort and refresh the souls of many. And what better Charitycharity imaginable, than by relieving the temporal wants of some few, to further the everlasting salvation of many? Oh what cause will their souls have to bless God to all eternity for your Charitycharity, who have been converted by the Ministryministry of those whom you have refreshed and supported in their work!

Reas. II▪ Anotheranother Reason may be taken from the consideration of the quality of the persons for whom I am pleading: Theythey are not so mean
as outwardly they appear. They whom you behold so poorly clad, walking so djectedly, being destitute of many outward comforts, are men endowed with many singular prerogatives and priviledges, not only above the rest of God's people; but likewise above the most glorious Angelsangels.

Compare them first with the people of God; they are called the Lord's Sheepsheep; Thesethese the Shepheards of the flock, Ezek. 34. 2. They Childrenchildren in God's family; Thesethese Spiritualspiritual Fathersfathers, who by the seed of the word beget men unto God, 1 Cor. 4. 15. Therefore the Spirit of God vouchsafeth them this dignity, to be called 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 , fellow-labourers with God.
Concerning Angelsangels; true it is that they and Ministersministers are fellow-servants, Rev. 22. 9. But yet Ministersministers have sundry prerogatives above them.
1. Angelsangels rejoyce at the conversion of a sinner, Luke 15. 10. But by the Ministery of Prophetsprophets sinners are converted unto God, Actact. 26. 18.
2. An Angelangel was sent to Cornelius, to advise him whither to go to be instructed: but a Ministerminister instructed him in the way of life, Actact. 10. 6. 34.

3. Was the word of Reconciliationreconciliation ever committed to Angelsangels? to Ministersministers it is committed, 2 Cor. 5. 18. It is observable, that the Embassage of Ministersministers is not simply 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 , Message, but
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 , the Gospel, the gladsome tydings of salvation by Jesus Christ, into which the Angelsangels themselves do desire to look and priepry, as the Apostle Peter expresseth, 1 Pet. 1. 12. The Lord hath also committed to his Ministersministers the administration of the Sacramentssacraments, which are the seals of his covenant, whereby all his precious promises are ratified, and confirmed unto us. So that as in respect of the rich treasures of God's Wordword committed to their dispensing, they are the Lord's Treasurerstreasurers: Soso in respect of the Sacramentssacraments, they are the Keepers of his great Sealseal. Ifif these Officersofficers be great under mortal Princesprinces, what are they under the King of Kings?

I have taken the liberty in a few words to set forth some of the priviledges of the Ministersministers of the Gospel; partly for the comfort and consolation of many of them under the present misery and poverty which they suffer, rather than to sin against their consciences: and partly for the incitation of others to afford them that double honour, which the Apostle calls for, 1 Tim. 5. 17. Namely, the honour of respect, and the honour of maintenance, that they suffer them not
to sink under their burthen, but afford them some seasonable succour and relief, suitable to their present wants and necessities.

Reas. III. Because Ministersministers are oftenest exposed to sufferings and distresses, and so have most need of relief. Thethe Bowbow of the Adversariesadversaries of Religionreligion is bent most against the Teachersteachers and Leadersleaders of the people. That word, 1 King. 22. 31. Fight neither with small or great, save only with the King of Israel, is often changed into, Fight neither with small or great, but only against the Prophetsprophets of the Lord. Smitesmite the Shepheards, and the Sheepsheep will be scattered. Experience enough tells the world who they are that are set in the Frontfront of the Battel, and who are the first that fall by the power of the Adversariesadversaries. And who should be most in the eye of Charitycharity, but those that are most in the eye of malice?

Besides, Forfor whose sakes is it that Ministersministers are so often brought so low? Is it not for your sakes, whose souls are dearer to them than their own substance? Is it not often upon this account, because they will be faithful to you, and will not keep silence, nor cease to watch over you, and to warn, and to instruct you from day to day?

Might they not save themselves more whole, if they would hold their peace, and let the Devildevil alone to have his will of you? For your sakes no doubt it is, that much of their sufferings come upon them; and shall they be forsaken by you? The truth is, it is upon this account a piece of Iusticejustice, as well as a piece of Charitycharity, to relieve and succour them; and so you may do two good works in one; the same alms may be both a work of righteousness, and a work of mercy.

Reas. IV. Your gratitude to God requireth a cheerful performance of this duty from you. Forfor wherein can you otherwise make a suitable return to God, for what he hath plentifully conferred on you, than by contributing some of your Temporals to them, from whom ye reap so much in Spirituals? Thethe Lord of his free grace and rich mercy hath abounded to you in these outward things; Hehe hath given you richly all things to enjoy. Yeayea, as the Psalmistpsalmist speaketh, Hehe hath loaded you with his benefits. Nownow, not to return some part of your estate to him, who hath given you all that you do enjoy, were ingratitude in the highest degree: Andand therefore how doth it concern you often to put the
Psalmistpsalmist's question to your selves, Whatwhat shall I render unto the Lord for all his benefits towards me? Psalmpsalm 116. 12. Surely one kindness deserveth another; as God hath been bountiful to you, sure you are very unworthy, if you be not bountiful to his. And how do you think he will take it at your hands? Will he ever say to you, Well done good and faithful Servantservant, thou hast been faithful, a good Stewardsteward of my many gifts? Oror, is it all one to you whether he say, Well done, or not?

And in regard you cannot directly and immediately requite him who is uncapable of being enriched by us; Mymy goodness extendeth not to thee, Psalmpsalm 16. 2. It will be your wisdom to expresseexpress your thankfulness to God by being kind to his poor relations. Now, who are nearer to God than his Ministersministers? whomWhom he hath appointed to stand in his room, to declare his mind unto his people; who are as the mouth of the people unto God; so God's mouth unto the people; who are the Messengersmessengers of the Lord of Hostshosts, by whose Ministryministry there is peace concluded, and reconciliation proclaimed between God and man. Surely what kindness you shewshow to these, he takes as done unto himself, Matth. 25. 40.

Reas. V. Your relieving the faithful Ministersministers of Christ, may in a sense be said tò have something more in it, than if you should shewshow your Charitycharity to himself, in his own person, as being a sign of greater love. Itit is but an ordinary thing to return kindness to our dearests friends; but to extend our good will to their relations, or servants for their sakes, is an evidence of much greater love. For if upon their account only we do good unto these; how much more would it be judged we should be ready to do it unto themselves, if they stood in need of our help? And so will Christ look upon it: Ourour bounty expressed to his Ministersministers he will receive as an evidence of our more abundant love unto him, which he will in no wise forget, nor suffer to go unrewarded.

Reas. VI. Suchsuch as relieve the poor Ministersministers of Christ, shall have their blessing, the benefit of their prayers unto God. Theythey will blessebless you however, though you have no blessing for them. Though you have not an alms for them, yet they will have a prayer for you. But their bowels being refreshed by you, you may expect that their heart will be the more enlarged for you; and this will be a far greater kindness than you can bestow on them. Your gift cannot be worth their fervent prayers. In this
respect it is much better to give, than to receive; because he that receives hath but a perishing alms; he that gives, receives an abiding blessing, the blessing of prayers.

Herein did the Apostle St. Paul, make a large requital to Onesiphorus for the kindness he shewedshowed to him in his imprisonment; as you may read, 2 Tim. 1. 16. The Lord give mercy unto the house of Onesiphorus, for he oft refreshed me, and was not ashamed of my chain. Asas if he had said, I received much comfort and refreshment from Onesiphorus, when I was in prison, for the which I beseech the Father of all mercies, to shewshow mercy unto him, and his, by blessing him, and his whole family, with all blessings, both temporal, spiritual and eternal. And indeed what blessing can that man want, who hath a share in many Ministersministers prayers? whichWhich are available for the obtaining of all good things at the hand of God, as for themselves, so for others. Yea the very work of Charitycharity doth bespeak a blessing from God. As the blood of Abel is said to cry to the Lord for a curse or vengeance upon Cain: so every act of Charitycharity cryeth to God for a blessing upon the Charitablecharitable. Our very acts of Charitycharity in relieving the wants of the poor, and refreshing their bowels, do pray and cry to God for his blessing upon us and ours.

Reas. VI. Your Charitycharity to them will be hereafter rewarded with everlasting glory and happiness in the Kingdomkingdom of Heavenheaven. Thisthis reason our Saviour himselfehimself giveth in these words; Hehe that recieveth a Prophetprophet in the name of a Prophetprophet, shall receive a Prophetsprophets reward; whereby is meant that surpassing and excellent weight of glory, which cannot be expressed by the tongue of men or Angelsangels. Yea, by the reward of a Prophetprophet seemeth to be implyed the highest degree of heavenly glory. For Daniel 12: 3. It is said, Thatthat they that be wise, that is, the righteous, who are endowed with true spiritual wisdom, being lightned by the Spirit of God, shall shine as the brightness of the Firmamentfirmament; but they that turn many to righteousness, which is the work of Prophetsprophets, shall shine as the Starsstars for ever and ever.

Now by your bounty to the Prophetsprophets of God, you may come to partake of their reward. So that it is your own concernment to contribute liberally towards their relief. Not that your Charitycharity to them doth merit that glorious reward; but in regard of the promise of God made to all those, who do exercisethe same towards
his Ministersministers, it shall be truly given unto them.

div.head: For a word of Application.
div.p: Ohoh how should the consideration of these things stir up the hearts of all, especially such as have a blessing in their hand, an estate to give, to draw forth their souls, and reach forth their hands to the supply of these wanting servants of God. Surelysurely this is a time wherein Christ is trying your love to him, by your Charitycharity to them. Are you not concerned to make proof of your love to Christ? Have you not an opportunity before you, and a loud call from Heavenheaven to prove it in this way? Can you not hear him, that said once to Peter, John 21. 16. LovestLouest thou me? Feed my Sheepsheep. Cancan you not hear the same voice calling to you, LovestLouest thou me? Feed my Shepheards. Suresure thou art very deaf to the voice of the Providencesprovidences of this day, if thou do not hear this Callcall. And will you prove that you have no love to Christ? What do you else if you suffer his to starve, when you have wherewith to feed them?

Beloved, it is through God's free grace, and rich bounty, that you enjoy such plenty of outward good things, when many of his Ministersministers are in great want. What you have, you have recieved from him. Is it not then most just and reasonable, that you should return back some part of your estates unto God, by relieving his Ministersministers, in testimony of your love and thankfulness unto him for what you have? Hath God given you hundreds and thousands? andAnd will not you part with a few pounds or shillings when he calls aloud unto you for the same, as now he doth in these dayesdays? Though the earth be his, and the fulness thereof, yet (in a sense) he hath sometimes need of your estates. Matth. 25. 35. Christ telleth you of his wants, and shewethshoweth you how, and when he is relieved.

If you have any spiritual wisdom to discern times and seasons. youYou may know, that now Christ stands in need of your helping hand, now that so many of his Ministersministers are in want, for the testimony of a good conscience: Andand should you now deny him in his Ministersministers, I do verily believe, that if Christ were now upon earth, as when he first took our nature upon him, and in his own person should crave your relief, you would turn a deaf ear unto him.

Though for the present you enjoy manifold blessings; yet how easily can he pluck them out of your mouths, and if you will not perform your duty, thrust you down from among the givers, to take your place among the receivers! Certainly the communicating
a part is your best way to secure the remainder, and to season and sanctifiesanctify it to your more comfortable use.

Luke 11. 41. Saith our Saviour, Givegive alms of such things as you have, and behold all things are clean unto you; that is, lawful to be used. The metaphor is taken from the Lawlaw, whereby many things were counted unclean, and so unlawful for use; they might not be touched or meddled with. Yea by the inference of the Apostle; Givegive alms of such things as you have, and behold all things are clean unto you: Hehe seemeth to allude to another Riterite of the Lawlaw about Firstfirst-fruits, Tithestithes, and Free offerings, by giving which to the Lord, all the rest which they had were secured, sanctified and made clean. So that charitable men are they, who may with the more freedom, quietness and comfort use what they have. Who that hath any desire to be accepted and appoved of God, would not have his person, and the actions which he doth, and things which he possesseth to be clean? Whatsoever is unclean is odious and abominable in God's sight: unclean persons might not approach to God's Sanctuarysanctuary, nor meddle with sacred matters. If they were not cleansed, they were to be cut off from God's Peoplepeople, Numb. 19 20. Levit. 7. 20. andAnd every unclean thing was an abomination.

This thereforé must needs be a strong perswasive to put in practise the counsel of our Saviour, in Givinggiving alms of such things as we have, that so all things may be clean, and sanctified unto us. What's clean you may use with God's good leave and allowance: (clean things might be eaten) and where you have God's good leave, you may expect his blessing. It's sin to eat where God's portion is among it.

The truth is, it is the great mistake of many, to think that all their goods are their own, and that they are absolute Lords and Ownersowners of all which they possess: Whereaswhereas indeed they are rather Stewards, than Lords and Ownersowners of this worlds goods; all is the Lords. God of his infinite wisdom hath committed to some a greater portion of them, than to others, yet not to be impropriated to themselves, but they must give him his special part, to which his have as good a right as themselves unto the rest, saving only that they may not lay hands on it themselves, until you put it into their hands. But as they may not take it out of yours; so you may not keep it out of their hands. Thereforetherefore Solomon speaking of the right which the poor have to a part of rich mens estates,
saith, Prov. 3. 27. Withold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thy hand to do it. Soso that relieving the poor is not only an act of Mercymercy, left to our choice to do, or leave undone; but also, as I said before, an act of Iusticejustice, to the performance whereof we stand bound. Hence to give alms, and to do Righteousnessrighteousness and Iusticejustice, are oft in Scripture put the one for the other, both signifying the same thing. Therefore the Septuagint have rendredrendered the Hebrew word signifying Righteousnessrighteousness, in Deut. 24. 14. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 , alms deeds. Andand in Psalmpsalm. 112. 9. It is said, Hishis Righteousnessrighteousness endureth for ever; that is, his alms, or his mercifulness; as is clear from the foregoing words; Hehe hath dispersed, he hath given to the poor; his Righteousnessrighteousness endureth for ever: Wherebywhereby is implyed, that giving of alms is one special branch of that Righteousnessrighteousness and Iusticejustice we owe to our poor neighbours.

And darest thou yet hold it in thy hand? Wilt thou wrong the Almighty of his right, and rob his poor of their due? Ifif it be nothing with thee to be unmerciful, is it nothing neither to be a robber? aA robber of God? Will a man rob God? Mal. 3. 8. Dares any man be so wicked? How canst thou but expect that he will make a forcible entry upon thee, and take what is his own, and seal a Writ of Ejectmentejectment against thee, and turn thee out of all that ever thou hast? Look not to be long in quiet possession of what thou hast; but fear lest either God should take thine estate from thee, or thee from thine estate, and give thee thy portion with Dives, who because he denyed his crumbs to satisfiesatisfy poor Lazarus his hunger, was himself denyed a drop of cold water to quench his own heat and thirst, Luke 16. 23. Upon which words St. Austin thus glosseth, Ideo rogans Dives non exauditur in tormentis, quia rogantem pauperem non exaudivit. Thereforetherefore was not Dives heard when he prayed in torments because he hearkened not to the poor that begged of him, when he was upon the Earthearth. Aug. Serm. deDe Divite.
Let me add a few quickningquickening words to set home what hath been spoken, by these following Questionsquestions.
Quest. 1. Nownow at length, Whatwhat dost thou think of mercy and bounty to the poor?

1. Isis there not an excellency in it? Ohoh how much of God is there in it! Therethere is faith in it; Hehe that will cast his bread upon the waters, is it not a sure sign that he believes God, who hath said, that it shall be returned again? There's the love of God in it: Hehe that
sees his Brotherbrother in need, and shuttethshuteth up the bowels of his compassions from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him? Andand he that openeth his bowels, and draws forth his soul to God's hungry ones, who can deny but the love of God dwelleth in that man? Itit is the Imageimage of God's goodness. God is a merciful God, and his mercy is his glory; and this glory of God shineth forth in his merciful servants. Therethere is self-denyal in it. Selfself would keep all; flesh would hold back; it cannot spare for God; 'tis a sign that self is laid low, that the flesh is kept under, that the interest of God is the swaying interest, when whatever God will have, this self is not suffered to keep back. Is there so much of God in mercifulness, and is there not an excellency in it?
2. Isis there not a necessity of it? Shallshall the merciless ever obtain mercy? Canst thou hope for mercy who wilt shewshow no mercy.

Qu. 2. Whatwhat dost thou think of thy self? Artart thou merciful, or merciless? How dost thou find it? Is thine heart open? areAre thy bowels open? orOr are they still shut? Dost thou feel that heart of thine inclined and resolved to open thy hands, and to disperse, and that liberally the good things thou hast received, as a good Stewardsteward of the manifold gifts of God? Or dost thou yet feel that the door is shut, thine heart is hardned against shewingshowing kindness to the Lord? Give thy plain judgment, what thinkest thou? Art thou a merciful man, or merciless? andAnd if merciless, Howhow dost thou hope to obtain mercy?
Qu. 3. What dost thou think of thy worldly goods?

1. Areare they not thy Talentstalents, committed to thee for thy Lord's use? Mustmust thou not be accountable to him, how they have been laid out? Will it be a comfortable account when thou must bring in thy Billbill; so much for thy pride, so much for thine appetite, or all hoarded up for thy covetousness, and nothing or but little for God?

2. Areare they more worth than Treasurestreasures in Heavenheaven? Isis it more to thine advantage to be rich in this worlds goods, than to be rich in good works? Dost thou in good earnest judge, that thy laying up treasures on earth is better husbandry, than thy laying up in store for thy self a good foundation against the time to come?

Qu. 4. Whatwhat dost thou think of the state of many of the servants of God in this age? Areare there no wanting ones? noNo distressed ones? What neither amongst Ministersministers, nor Christians? Are they all provided for? Do not many of them eat the bread, and drink the waters
of affliction? Is it not very strait and very short with them? Do but enquire after their condition, and thou wilt find it so. Art thou one of those that carest not how it fares with the poor friends of Christ? Are they not worth the enquiring, and looking after? orOr at least, Isis not he worthy, whose they are, and whom they serve? Is not Christ worthy, for whose sake thou should'st shewshow kindness to his? How will he take thy neglect of them? Remember that word, Matth. 25. 45. Inasmuch as ye did it not to these, ye did it not to me.

Qu. 5. Whatwhat wilt thou do for the future? Whatwhat shall be the success of these few words that are written for thy learning? What art thou resolved upon? forFor mercy, or for cruelty? Consult thine own heart; lay not by this little Bookbook, till thou art come to a resolution one way or other, either to accept, or reject this counsel, which in the name of the Lord is offered thee for thy good. Oh shewshow thy self a man in whose soul Christ hath an interest, and so great an interest, that thou wilt do any thing at his word; pity at his word, relieve at his word, give, lend, feed, cloathe, refresh the bowels of his needy ones: Letlet thy soul say, Lord, at thy word I will do it: here's my bread, and my flesh, and my money, command what thou wilt of it, I will not say thee nay. Thou hast given me a large portion, and every one of thy servants that thou appointest to receive it, shall have their part; for thy sake, Lord, they shall have it. Thine I am, and thine is all that I have; shewshow me thy pleasure, how much, and how often, and where, and to whom I shall bestow it, and through the grace of God there it shall go.

Friend, Wiltwilt thou say thus? Wilt thou in the presence of the Lord come to this gracious resolution? orOr canst thou yet find in thine heart to deny thy Lord, and continue to be as hard-hearted, and close-handed as thou wer't wont to be? Dare not to say, Lord, my goods are mine own, I owe thee nothing: Dreaddread such thoughts, that how much soever thou hast, the servants of Christ shall be nothing the better for it.

Once again consider, thou art put to this choice, either to accept of the counsel of Christ, or to reject it; which of the two wilt thou do? If thou resolvest not on mercy, and liberality, thou rejectest the word of the Lord; and if thou rejectest his word, thou rejectest the Lord, and therein sayest, Hehe shall be no Lord for me. But if thou acceptest, then go, and do accordingly: Letlet the hunger, and the thirst, and the nakedness; the wants and distresses of his servants
feel in that relief they shall receive from thee, that thou art a man to whom the Lord hath not spoken in vain. Let them feel it presently, and let them feel it constantly; this year, and the next year, and the next, even whilst they have need to receive, and thou hast it by thee to give. This do, and the Lord accept thee; remember all thy offering, and accept all thy sacrifices; the Lord hear thee in the day of thy trouble; the name of the God of IacobJacob defend thee: Thethe Lord grant thee according to thine own heart, and fulfill all thy counsel: Thethe Lord remember thee with the favour he beareth unto his children, and visit thee with his salvation.
